Its chloride anion oxidation at 4.0 V is a possible risk, but the cathode-side contact is expected to be more stable than with fluoride or phosphate.

proposals.hypothesis: Li2O is the simplest Li-rich oxide: it has no polyanion network and no reducible cation, so it has few non-Li atoms for the penalty to be spread over. Its oxide anion is thermodynamically stable against the sulfide and chloride electrolyte, and it is wide-gap and oxidatively stable at 4.0 V on the LiCoO2 side. It is a chemically distinct family from the phosphate, fluoride, chloride, zirconate and borate coatings tested so far.
proposals.motivation: The best penalty so far is about 0.056 (bin 2), and no coating meets the 0.05 threshold. Phosphate, fluoride, chloride, Zr-oxide, borate and aluminosilicate coatings all gave larger sulfide-side penalties, so a simple Li2O oxide is the next untested family.

proposal.hypothesis: Li3PO4 is a wide-gap, electronically insulating oxyanion lithium salt. It shares the PO4 chemistry of the sulfide electrolyte's phosphorus network and is widely used as a thin cathode/sulfide interlayer. It should be chemically compatible with both LiCoO2 and Li6PS5Cl, and its high oxidative stability should help at 4.0 V.

LiF is a very wide-gap, highly electronegative, Li-rich fluoride that is thermodynamically inert toward both the sulfide electrolyte and the oxide cathode. Fluoride anions resist oxidation at 4.0 V and form no P-S or Co redox products, so it should avoid the reactive contact products seen for Li3PO4. It is a known cathode-coating material and should be insulating with a band gap well above 2 eV.
proposal.motivation: Li3PO4 was insulating and wide-gap but its sulfide-side contact decomposed (penalty 0.337 eV/non-Li atom, bin 16, not acceptable). A chemically different, fluoride-based coating is needed to reduce the interfacial reaction penalty.

proposal.hypothesis: Li2MgCl4 is a wide-gap chloride Li salt. Its Cl- anions are chemically matched to the Cl in Li6PS5Cl, so the sulfide-side interface should avoid the P-S-O or P-S-F reduction products seen for the oxide and fluoride coatings. Mg2+ is hard to reduce, so it should not form reactive metal sulfides at low potential. Its chloride anion oxidation at 4.0 V is a possible risk, but the cathode-side contact is expected to be more stable than with fluoride or phosphate.
proposal.motivation: Li3PO4 and LiF both gave sulfide-side contact decomposition with penalties around 0.31 to 0.34 eV per non-Li atom, both outside the acceptance threshold of 0.05. A chloride-based coating matched to the electrolyte's halide chemistry is a different family that may reduce this interfacial penalty.

proposal.hypothesis: LiZr2(PO4)3 is a NASICON-type phosphate in which the Zr4+ centers are highly resistant to reduction. Sulfide-side reactions in the earlier trials were driven by P/S/Cl or F redox chemistry, so a Zr-based phosphate framework may avoid the reactive P-S-O and P-S-F products. Its wide band gap should keep it insulating, and it is stable toward oxidation at 4.0 V on the LiCoO2 side.
proposal.motivation: Li3PO4, LiF and Li2MgCl4 were all insulating and wide-gap, but each showed sulfide-side contact decomposition with penalties of 0.19 to 0.34 eV per non-Li atom, far above the 0.05 threshold. A Zr4+-based oxide, which is more reduction-resistant than the single-anion coatings tried so far, is the next chemically distinct test.

proposal.hypothesis: Li6Zr2O7 is a Li2O-rich zirconate. Zr4+ is hard to reduce, and the earlier LiZr2(PO4)3 trial had the lowest sulfide-side penalty so far (0.19 eV/non-Li atom), which suggests Zr-centred frameworks resist the P/S/Cl redox products. Relative to the phosphate, this oxide has no P to form P-S or P-Cl products, and its high Li content may keep the interphase Li-rich.
